notes:
SECOND-PASS CORRECTIONS FROM ADVERSARIAL REVIEW (both applied below): (1) Hebrews 11:32 KJV reads "Gedeon, and Barak, and Samson, and Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel" — Deborah is NOT named in that verse. Barak's funFacts and this notes field now say only that Barak (not Deborah) appears there. (2) Jair the Gileadite, one of the five minor judges (Judges 10:3-5), is flagged explicitly as a likely naming collision with the earlier, distinct "Jair the son of Manasseh" credited with taking/naming the towns of Havothjair in Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14 (see also the separate, only partly-reconcilable Jair genealogy at 1 Chronicles 2:21-22 via Hezron/Segub). These are two different men separated by centuries (conquest generation vs. judges era) who share both a name and an association with "Havothjair" — Judges 10:4 says Jair's 30 sons' 30 cities "are called Havothjair unto this day," which does not itself claim he originated the name; the identical name is the likely source of conflation. Do not identify them as the same person.

ADDITIONAL NAMING COLLISIONS FLAGGED THIS PASS (per the standing instruction to re-scan every name used): Gera (Ehud's father, Judges 3:15) reuses a Benjamite ancestor/clan name also found in Genesis 46:21 and 1 Chronicles 8:3,5,7 — different individuals, likely the same recurring clan name. Eglon (Judges 3) is a king's personal name that also happens to be an unrelated Canaanite city name (Joshua 10:3,34-37; 12:12; 15:39) ruled by a different king (Debir) — person vs. place, not a person collision, but easy to conflate. Jabin king of Hazor (Judges 4:2,17,23-24, Sisera's overlord) shares a name and title with the earlier Jabin king of Hazor defeated by Joshua (Joshua 11:1-11) — treated here as a distinct, later individual (possibly a recurring dynastic/throne name at Hazor), not the same king Joshua fought generations earlier. Tola (Judges 10:1) shares a name with Tola son of Issachar, an actual son of the patriarch Issachar (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:23; 1 Chronicles 7:1-2) — the judge, "a man of Issachar," is almost certainly a much later descendant bearing the ancestral name, not the same person. Tola's father Puah and grandfather Dodo likewise reuse names found elsewhere for different people (Puah/Puvah son of Issachar, Genesis 46:13/Numbers 26:23; Puah the Hebrew midwife, Exodus 1:15; Dodo of Bethlehem, father of the mighty man Elhanan, 2 Samuel 23:24). Elon the judge (Judges 12:11-12, "a Zebulonite") shares a name with both Elon the Hittite, Esau's father-in-law (Genesis 26:34) and Elon son of Zebulun (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26) — different individuals in different eras, though the tribal echo with the latter is notable. Abdon the judge (Judges 12:13-15) shares a name with the Levitical city of Abdon (Joshua 21:30; 1 Chronicles 6:74) and with unrelated Benjamite men named Abdon (1 Chronicles 8:23; 9:36). Jether, Gideon's son (Judges 8:20), shares a name with Jethro/Jether, Moses' father-in-law (called "Jether" in Exodus 4:18) — unrelated, centuries apart. Gershom, father of Jonathan the Levite priest (Judges 18:30), shares a name with Moses' own son Gershom (Exodus 2:22) and with Levi's son Gershon/Gershom (Genesis 46:11; 1 Chronicles 6:16-17) — compounded by a separate, well-documented textual crux (below). Jonathan the Levite priest (Judges 18:30) shares a name with the far more famous Jonathan son of Saul — unrelated, different tribe and era. Sisera (Judges 4) shares a name with "the children of Sisera," a family of Nethinim listed among the exiles returning under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55) — almost certainly an unrelated later namesake, not descendants of Sisera the Canaanite general. Gilead, given as Jephthah's father's name (Judges 11:1-2), is also the standard eponymous/clan name for the whole Gileadite region and lineage (Numbers 26:29; 1 Chronicles 7:14) — hedged below as possibly a clan designation rather than one specific individual.

OTHER HEDGED CRUXES (flagged rather than resolved): Othniel's relationship to Caleb ("Caleb's younger brother," Joshua 15:17/Judges 1:13) is grammatically ambiguous between Othniel and his father Kenaz. Deborah as "the wife of Lapidoth" (Judges 4:4) may be a proper name or a Hebrew epithet ("woman of torches") — hedged. Heber the Kenite's clan descent "of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses" (Judges 4:11) inherits Hobab's own debated relationship to Moses (father-in-law vs. brother-in-law across Exodus 2:18/3:1 and Numbers 10:29). Barak's possible identity with "Bedan" in 1 Samuel 12:11 is a long-noted but unresolved crux, not asserted here. Abimelech's father Gideon is called "Jerubbesheth" in 2 Samuel 11:21 — a variant/euphemistic form of "Jerubbaal," flagged. Jonathan the Levite's grandfather is given in the KJV as "Manasseh" (Judges 18:30), but the Hebrew has a raised/suspended letter (nun) widely regarded by scholars as an intentional scribal alteration of "Moses" to obscure a direct Mosaic link to this idolatrous priesthood — the KJV's actual reading ("Manasseh") is used as the primary datum; Mosaic descent is NOT asserted as fact. The fate of Jephthah's daughter (literal sacrifice vs. lifelong dedicated virginity) is a genuine, long-standing interpretive crux, hedged rather than resolved. The concubine's description in Judges 19:2 ("played the whore against him") reflects the KJV's own wording, which is quoted directly per project rules; some versions/scholars render the underlying Hebrew differently (e.g., anger/estrangement) — flagged, not resolved. Delilah's nationality is never stated in the text (Judges 16:4 only places her "in the valley of Sorek") and is not asserted here despite common assumption that she was Philistine. Phinehas in Judges 20:28 shares the exact genealogy (son of Eleazar, son of Aaron) given for the Phinehas of Numbers 25 and Joshua 22, suggesting continuity, but his appearance this late in the book (which closes with the "no king in Israel" appendix, chapters 17-21, widely read as chronologically earlier than the book's final placement suggests) is noted as a common observation, not asserted as settled internal chronology.

SCHEMA CONSISTENCY SELF-CHECK: every managerId used in scribeTiers (othniel, ehud, shamgar, deborah, barak, jael, gideon, abimelech, tola, jair_gileadite, jephthah, ibzan, elon, abdon, samson, delilah, micah, levite_of_ephraim, phinehas) has a matching characters[] entry with role "manager". Every parentManagerId used by a submanager (ehud, deborah, barak, jael, gideon x5, abimelech x4, jephthah, samson x3, micah x2, levite_of_ephraim x3) resolves to one of those same manager ids. No character holds both a scribeTier and a parentManagerId.

genealogyLists.danite_spies: Five unnamed Danite men sent to spy out Laish before the tribal migration north (Judges 18:2, 7-10).
genealogyLists.danite_600_men: Six hundred armed Danite men who migrated north, absorbed Micah's priest Jonathan and his idols en route, and destroyed and resettled Laish as Dan (Judges 18:11-29). No individuals besides Jonathan are named.
genealogyLists.philistine_lords: The unnamed 'lords of the Philistines' who bribed Delilah with 1,100 pieces of silver each to learn the secret of Samson's strength (Judges 16:5).
genealogyLists.men_of_gibeah: The unnamed 'certain sons of Belial' of Gibeah who surrounded the old man's house and abused the Levite's concubine to death (Judges 19:22-26).
genealogyLists.jephthahs_brothers: Jephthah's unnamed half-brothers (sons of Gilead's wife) who drove him out, denying him inheritance as the son of a harlot (Judges 11:1-2).
genealogyLists.jabeshgilead_virgins: 400 virgins of Jabeshgilead spared from the city's destruction and given as wives to the surviving Benjamites (Judges 21:8-14); the rest of Jabeshgilead was destroyed for not joining Israel's muster/oath.
genealogyLists.shiloh_daughters: Unnamed dancing daughters of Shiloh seized as wives for the remaining unmatched Benjamites during a yearly feast (Judges 21:19-23).
genealogyLists.benjamite_survivors: 600 Benjamite men who survived the civil war by fleeing to the rock Rimmon for four months (Judges 20:47).
genealogyLists.ephraimite_shibboleth_dead: 42,000 Ephraimites killed at the fords of Jordan for mispronouncing 'Shibboleth' during the conflict following Jephthah's judgeship (Judges 12:5-6).
genealogyLists.midianite_host: The vast, unnamed Midianite/Amalekite/'children of the east' coalition described as innumerable, 'like grasshoppers for multitude,' defeated by Gideon's 300 (Judges 7:12).

characters.name: Othniel

genealogy.note: Called 'Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother' (Joshua 15:17; Judges 1:13) — the Hebrew is ambiguous about whether Othniel or Kenaz is the one described as Caleb's brother; his exact relation to Caleb (brother vs. nephew) is hedged, not settled by the text.

funFacts: First deliverer named in the judges cycle: Israel served Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia 8 years before Othniel delivered them and the land had rest 40 years (Judges 3:8,11).
Also appears in Joshua 15:16-19/Judges 1:12-15 winning Achsah's hand by capturing Kirjathsepher (Debir), then being granted springs of water at her request.

verses.note: Raised up as Israel's first judge/deliverer; 'the Spirit of the LORD came upon him.'
Earlier episode establishing his marriage to Achsah.

characters.name: Ehud

genealogy.note: A Benjamite. 'Gera' also names an ancestral/clan figure in Genesis 46:21 and later Benjamite men in 1 Chronicles 8:3,5,7 — likely the same recurring clan name across generations, not evidence of direct identity with Ehud's father.

funFacts: Explicitly 'lefthanded' (Judges 3:15, literally 'shut of his right hand'), which let him hide a two-edged dagger on his right thigh past Eglon's guards.
After killing Eglon he rallied Israel at Mount Ephraim and led the defeat of Moab; the land had rest 80 years (Judges 3:27-30), the longest peace of any judge cycle.

verses.note: Delivers a 'secret errand' to Eglon and kills him with a concealed dagger.
Leads Israel to defeat Moab at the fords of Jordan.

characters.name: Eglon
characters.perkNote: Folded in as Ehud's tier antagonist — his oppressive tribute is the 'cost' Ehud's blade removes.

genealogy.note: King of Moab; not to be confused with the unrelated Canaanite city of Eglon (Joshua 10:3,34-37; 12:12; 15:39), ruled by a different king, Debir, generations earlier — a place/person name overlap, not a person collision.

funFacts: Allied with Ammon and Amalek to oppress Israel 18 years (Judges 3:12-14).
Described bluntly as 'a very fat man' (Judges 3:17), a detail the narrative uses for grim comic effect in his death scene.

verses.note: Oppresses Israel 18 years.
Physical description before Ehud's audience with him.

characters.name: Shamgar

genealogy.note: 'Son of Anath' may indicate a literal father or, per some readings, an association with a place name (e.g., Bethanath) — hedged rather than asserted as a literal genealogical father.

funFacts: Slew 600 Philistines with an ox goad and 'also delivered Israel' (Judges 3:31) — his entire account is a single verse.
Referenced again in the Song of Deborah as a chronological marker for a time when 'the highways were unoccupied' (Judges 5:6).

verses.note: His sole narrative verse.
Retrospective mention in the Song of Deborah.

characters.name: Deborah

genealogy.note: 'The wife of Lapidoth' (Judges 4:4) is debated — it may name her husband, or be a Hebrew idiom ('woman of torches/flames') describing her rather than a literal spousal name; hedged.

funFacts: A prophetess who 'judged Israel at that time,' dwelling under 'the palm tree of Deborah' between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4:4-5).
Co-composes the victory Song of Deborah with Barak in Judges 5, one of the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible.
Barak — not Deborah — is later named in Hebrews 11:32's roll of faith ('Gedeon, and Barak, and Samson, and Jephthae'); Deborah herself does not appear in that verse.

verses.note: Summons Barak and prophesies the LORD will sell Sisera 'into the hand of a woman.'
The Song of Deborah, sung with Barak.

characters.name: Jabin king of Hazor
characters.perkNote: The oppressor whose 20-year rule (via his captain Sisera) is the burden Deborah's judgeship relieves.

genealogy.note: Shares his name and title with an earlier, distinct Jabin king of Hazor defeated by Joshua (Joshua 11:1-11) — treated here as a later, different individual (possibly a recurring dynastic name at Hazor), not the same king.

funFacts: Had 900 chariots of iron and 'mightily oppressed' Israel 20 years through his army captain Sisera (Judges 4:2-3).

verses.note: Introduces his oppression and Sisera's command.
Israel eventually 'subdued Jabin king of Canaan.'

characters.name: Barak

genealogy.note: No further genealogical detail is given beyond his father's name.

funFacts: From Kedeshnaphtali; refuses to march against Sisera unless Deborah goes with him, prompting her prophecy that the honor of the victory would instead go to a woman (Judges 4:8-9) — fulfilled by Jael, not Deborah.
Barak is named in Hebrews 11:32 among the roll of faith: 'Gedeon, and Barak, and Samson, and Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel' — Deborah is not named in that verse.
Possibly identified by some readers with 'Bedan' in 1 Samuel 12:11's list of judges — a long-noted but unresolved textual crux, not asserted here.

verses.note: Leads 10,000 men to Mount Tabor and routs Sisera's army.
Named in the roll of faith alongside Gideon, Samson, and Jephthah.

characters.name: Sisera
characters.perkNote: The commander whose 900 iron chariots represent the military obstacle Barak's tier overcomes.

genealogy.note: A family called 'the children of Sisera' appears among the Nethinim returning from exile (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55) — almost certainly an unrelated later namesake, not descendants of this Sisera.

funFacts: Captain of Jabin's army with 900 chariots of iron (Judges 4:2-3).
Flees on foot to Jael's tent after his army's defeat, expecting refuge because of peace between Jabin and Heber's clan (Judges 4:17).

verses.note: His army routed at Barak's charge.
Killed in Jael's tent.

characters.name: Jael

genealogy.note: No parentage given in the text; identified only by marriage.

funFacts: Kills Sisera by driving a tent peg through his temple while he sleeps, fulfilling Deborah's prophecy that he would fall 'into the hand of a woman' (Judges 4:21).
Praised in the Song of Deborah as 'blessed above women... blessed shall she be above women in the tent' (Judges 5:24).

verses.note: Kills Sisera and shows Barak the body.
Celebrated in the Song of Deborah.

characters.name: Heber the Kenite
characters.perkNote: His household's peace with Jabin is what draws Sisera to the tent in the first place — folded in as context supporting Jael's tier.

genealogy.note: Judges 4:11 links his clan to 'the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses' — Hobab's exact relation to Moses (father-in-law vs. brother-in-law) is itself debated across Exodus 2:18/3:1 and Numbers 10:29; hedged.

funFacts: Had separated from other Kenites and was 'at peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber' (Judges 4:17), which is why Sisera sought refuge in his camp.

verses.note: Introduces his Kenite/Hobab lineage.
His peace with Jabin.

characters.name: Gideon

spouses: an unnamed concubine in Shechem, mother of Abimelech (Judges 8:31)
children: and 68 other unnamed sons (Judges 8:30-31, 'threescore and ten sons of his body begotten')
genealogy.note: Of the tribe of Manasseh, clan of Abiezer; also called Jerubbaal after tearing down Baal's altar (Judges 6:32), and 'Jerubbesheth' in the later reference at 2 Samuel 11:21 — a variant/euphemistic form of the same name.

funFacts: Reduces his army from 32,000 to 300 men via the water-lapping test before the night raid on Midian (Judges 7:2-7).

Refuses kingship when offered it: 'I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you' (Judges 8:23) — yet afterward makes a golden ephod at Ophrah that 'became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house' (Judges 8:27), a detail the text does not soften.

verses.note: Called by the angel of the LORD; 'I am the least in my father's house.'
The trumpets-and-pitchers night raid.
Refuses kingship, then makes the ephod.

characters.name: Joash the Abiezrite
characters.perkNote: Defends his son from the mob demanding his death, buying Gideon the standing that lets his tier's story continue.

genealogy.note: No further genealogical detail is given for Joash himself in the text.

funFacts: Owns the altar of Baal and the Asherah/grove that Gideon tears down by night (Judges 6:25-27).
Defends Gideon before the men of the city: 'Will ye plead for Baal?... if he be a god, let him plead for himself' (Judges 6:31) — the origin of Gideon's other name, Jerubbaal (6:32).

verses.note: His altar torn down; his speech saves Gideon's life.

characters.name: Purah
characters.perkNote: Accompanies Gideon into the enemy camp, steadying him before the raid.

genealogy.note: No genealogical detail given; identified only as Gideon's servant.

funFacts: Gideon's servant/young man who goes with him down to overhear a Midianite's dream of a barley cake overturning the camp, which encourages Gideon before the attack (Judges 7:10-15).

verses.note: Accompanies Gideon to the edge of the camp.

characters.name: Jether
characters.perkNote: Gideon's firstborn, given the chance to share in the victory over Zebah and Zalmunna.

genealogy.note: Distinct from Jethro/Jether, Moses' father-in-law (called 'Jether' in Exodus 4:18) — an unrelated name overlap, centuries apart.

funFacts: Commanded by Gideon to kill the captured kings Zebah and Zalmunna, but 'the youth drew not his sword: for he feared, because he was yet a youth' (Judges 8:20).

verses.note: His refusal to act.

characters.name: Zebah and Zalmunna
characters.perkNote: The captured Midianite kings whose deaths close out Gideon's campaign; kept as one entry since the text never differentiates their words or fate.

genealogy.note: Text gives them identical dialogue and an identical fate throughout (Judges 8:5-21), so they are catalogued together rather than as separate individuals, per the project's rule against inventing an undifferentiated distinction.

funFacts: Kings of Midian pursued and captured by Gideon beyond Jordan; their reply about the men they killed at Tabor ('As the man is, so is his strength') provokes Gideon to kill them himself after Jether refuses (Judges 8:18-21).

verses.note: Captured after their army is routed.
Killed by Gideon personally.

characters.name: Oreb and Zeeb
characters.perkNote: Midianite princes whose capture by Ephraim, prompted by Gideon's call, is memorialized in the landscape itself.

genealogy.note: Always paired identically in every scriptural mention (Judges 7:25; 8:3; Psalm 83:11; Isaiah 10:26), so catalogued as one entry.

funFacts: Captured and killed by the men of Ephraim at places subsequently named for them — 'the rock Oreb' and 'the winepress of Zeeb' (Judges 7:25); their heads are brought to Gideon.
Remembered later in Psalm 83:11 ('make their nobles like Oreb and like Zeeb').

verses.note: Captured and killed by Ephraim.
Later poetic remembrance.

characters.name: Abimelech

genealogy.note: No wife or children of his own are named in the text.

funFacts: Persuades the men of Shechem to make him king and murders 69 of his 70 half-brothers on one stone at Ophrah; only Jotham escapes (Judges 9:1-5).

Killed at Thebez when 'a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull' (Judges 9:53); he has his armorbearer run him through so it 'not be said of me, A woman slew him' (9:54) — yet 2 Samuel 11:21 remembers the episode exactly that way anyway.

verses.note: Murders his brothers and is made king.
After 3 years, God sends an evil spirit between him and Shechem.
His death at Thebez.

characters.name: Jotham
characters.perkNote: Family member who opposes rather than supports the tier's major — his curse against Abimelech and Shechem is the narrative 'cost' that eventually comes due.

genealogy.note: No further genealogical detail beyond his father Gideon.

funFacts: The youngest son of Jerubbaal and sole survivor of the massacre at Ophrah, having hidden himself (Judges 9:5).
Delivers the fable of the trees from atop Mount Gerizim as a curse against Shechem and Abimelech (Judges 9:7-20), then flees to Beer; the fable's curse is explicitly fulfilled at 9:56-57.

verses.note: Escapes the massacre.
The fable of the trees.

characters.name: Gaal the son of Ebed
characters.perkNote: Leads the Shechemite uprising against Abimelech, forcing the confrontation that eventually costs Abimelech Shechem entirely.

genealogy.note: No further genealogical detail given.

funFacts: Incites Shechem to rebel against Abimelech: 'Who is Abimelech... that we should serve him?' (Judges 9:28).
Defeated and driven out of the city by Zebul, Abimelech's officer, before Abimelech's own assault on Shechem (Judges 9:34-41).

verses.note: Incites rebellion.
Defeated and expelled by Zebul.

characters.name: Zebul
characters.perkNote: Abimelech's loyal officer in Shechem who secretly warns him of Gaal's plot and times the counterattack.

genealogy.note: No genealogical detail given; identified only by office.

funFacts: 'Ruler of the city' of Shechem under Abimelech; secretly sends messengers warning Abimelech of Gaal's conspiracy and advises him on the timing of his attack (Judges 9:30-33).

verses.note: Warns Abimelech and advises his strategy.

characters.name: The Woman of Thebez
characters.perkNote: The unnamed figure whose single act ends Abimelech's brief, violent reign.

genealogy.note: Unnamed in the text ('a certain woman,' Judges 9:53); descriptive id used rather than an invented name.

funFacts: Casts a piece of a millstone from the tower wall onto Abimelech's head, fatally cracking his skull (Judges 9:53).

verses.note: Her decisive action.

characters.name: Tola

genealogy.note: Grandfather given as Dodo (Judges 10:1). Shares his name with Tola son of Issachar, an actual son of the patriarch Issachar (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:23; 1 Chronicles 7:1-2) — the judge, described as 'a man of Issachar,' is almost certainly a much later descendant carrying the ancestral name, not the same individual. 'Puah' likewise reuses a name found for Issachar's son Puah/Puvah (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:23) and for the Hebrew midwife Puah (Exodus 1:15); 'Dodo' reuses a name found for the father of David's mighty man Elhanan (2 Samuel 23:24) — different people in each case.

funFacts: Rose 'to defend Israel' after Abimelech's death, dwelling in Shamir in Mount Ephraim; judged Israel 23 years (Judges 10:1-2).

verses.note: His entire, brief account.

characters.name: Jair the Gileadite

genealogy.note: FLAGGED NAMING COLLISION: this Jair, a judge of Israel (Judges 10:3-5), is frequently and incorrectly conflated with the earlier, distinct 'Jair the son of Manasseh,' who took/named the towns of Havothjair generations earlier during the conquest under Moses (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14). A further, only partly reconcilable genealogy for a 'Jair' appears at 1 Chronicles 2:21-22 via Hezron and Segub. These are best treated as separate individuals centuries apart who happen to share a name and an association with the place name Havothjair; Judges 10:4 itself only says the 30 cities of Jair's 30 sons 'are called Havothjair unto this day,' not that this Jair originated the name.

funFacts: Judged Israel 22 years; his 30 sons rode on 30 ass colts and held 30 cities in Gilead (Judges 10:3-4).
Died and was buried in Camon (Judges 10:5).

verses.note: His entire account.
The earlier, distinct Jair son of Manasseh — flagged collision, not the same person.
Further detail on the earlier Jair son of Manasseh.

characters.name: Jephthah

children: an unnamed daughter, his only child (Judges 11:34)
genealogy.note: 'Gilead' as Jephthah's father's name is itself ambiguous — 'Gilead' is also the standard eponymous/clan name for the whole Gileadite region and lineage (Numbers 26:29; 1 Chronicles 7:14), so it may denote a specific individual or function as a clan/regional designation; hedged rather than resolved.

funFacts: Driven out by his half-brothers as 'the son of a strange woman' (Judges 11:2), he became a mighty man of valour leading 'vain men' from the land of Tob before Gilead's elders recalled him to lead against Ammon (Judges 11:3-11).
Vows to sacrifice 'whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me' if granted victory (Judges 11:30-31); his own daughter comes out first.
Coins the 'Shibboleth' test against fleeing Ephraimites at the Jordan fords, in which 42,000 died for mispronouncing the word (Judges 12:5-6).

verses.note: His birth and expulsion.
The vow.
His daughter's fate.
The Shibboleth test.

characters.name: Jephthah's Daughter
characters.perkNote: Her acceptance of her father's vow becomes an annual commemoration among Israel's daughters.

genealogy.note: Unnamed in the text; described only as his 'only child' (Judges 11:34).

funFacts: Comes out to meet her father with timbrels and dances after his victory, unknowingly fulfilling his vow (Judges 11:34).

Requests two months to 'bewail my virginity' upon the mountains with her companions before the vow is carried out (Judges 11:37-38); whether this means she was put to death or set apart to perpetual virginity/service is a long-debated, unresolved interpretive crux — not settled here.
Her fate becomes the origin of a yearly four-day custom of Israel's daughters lamenting her (Judges 11:39-40).

verses.note: Meets her father and accepts the vow's outcome.
Her request and the resulting custom.

characters.name: Ibzan

genealogy.note: Text says only 'of Bethlehem' without specifying which — likely Bethlehem-judah, but a lesser-known Bethlehem in Zebulun is also attested (Joshua 19:15); hedged rather than assumed.

funFacts: Had 30 sons and 30 daughters; sent his daughters out in marriage and brought in 30 women from elsewhere for his sons (Judges 12:9).
Judged Israel 7 years, died, and was buried in Bethlehem (Judges 12:9-10).

verses.note: His entire account.

characters.name: Elon

genealogy.note: Shares his name with Elon the Hittite, father-in-law of Esau (Genesis 26:34), and with Elon son of Zebulun (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26) — different individuals in different eras; the tribal echo with the latter (Elon the judge is himself 'a Zebulonite') is notable but not evidence of identity.

funFacts: Judged Israel 10 years, died, and was buried in Aijalon in the country of Zebulun (Judges 12:11-12).

verses.note: His entire account.

characters.name: Abdon

children: thirty 'nephews' (i.e. grandsons — archaic KJV usage of 'nephew' from Latin nepos, not siblings' sons; Judges 12:14)
genealogy.note: Shares his name with the Levitical city of Abdon (Joshua 21:30; 1 Chronicles 6:74) and with unrelated Benjamite men named Abdon (1 Chronicles 8:23; 9:36).

funFacts: His 40 sons and 30 grandsons rode on 70 ass colts (Judges 12:14).
Judged Israel 8 years; died and was buried in Pirathon in Ephraim, 'in the mount of the Amalekites' (Judges 12:13-15).

verses.note: His entire account.

characters.name: Samson

genealogy.note: Of the tribe of Dan, from Zorah. His 20-year judgeship (Judges 15:20; 16:31) is sometimes discussed as overlapping the priesthood of Eli and early life of Samuel per 1 Samuel — a commonly noted chronological observation, not asserted here from the text of Judges itself.

funFacts: Announced before conception by the angel of the LORD as a Nazarite (KJV spelling) unto God from the womb (Judges 13:5,7).

Kills a young lion barehanded, later finds honey in its carcass, and poses the riddle 'Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness' at his wedding feast (Judges 14:5-14).
Pulls down the temple of Dagon in his death, killing more Philistines than in his whole life (Judges 16:29-30).

verses.note: His birth and early stirring of the Spirit.
He judged Israel twenty years.
His death at Dagon's temple.

characters.name: Manoah
characters.perkNote: Father who receives the angelic announcement of Samson's birth and offers sacrifice in response.

genealogy.note: Of Zorah, of the family of the Danites (Judges 13:2).

funFacts: After the angel of the LORD ascends in the flame of his offering, fears 'We shall surely die, because we have seen God' (Judges 13:19-22).

verses.note: Introduced as a Danite of Zorah.
His fearful response to the theophany.

characters.name: Manoah's Wife
characters.perkNote: Receives the initial angelic annunciation of Samson's birth and offers the calmer, wiser theological read of the encounter.

genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout; described only as 'his wife' (Judges 13:2) and 'the woman' (13:9-10).

funFacts: Barren, receives the angel's announcement of Samson's birth and the Nazarite instructions before Manoah is included (Judges 13:3-5).
Reassures Manoah after the theophany that the LORD would not have accepted their offering or shown them these things if He meant to kill them (Judges 13:23).

verses.note: Receives the first angelic announcement.
Her reassurance to Manoah.

characters.name: Samson's Timnite Wife
characters.perkNote: Her extraction of the riddle's answer under threat directly costs Samson the wager and 30 men's lives.

genealogy.father: an unnamed Philistine man of Timnath
genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout, called only 'Samson's wife' or 'the woman.'

funFacts: Weeps before Samson seven days until he tells her the riddle's answer under threat that her people would burn her father's house (Judges 14:15-17).
Given to Samson's companion after the wedding feast (Judges 14:20); later burned to death along with her father by the Philistines in retaliation for Samson's fox-and-firebrand revenge (Judges 15:6).

verses.note: Extracts the riddle's answer.
Her death.

characters.name: Delilah

genealogy.note: Text places her only 'in the valley of Sorek' (Judges 16:4) and never states her nationality; the common assumption that she was Philistine is not asserted directly by the text and is treated here as unconfirmed.

funFacts: Bribed by the Philistine lords with 1,100 pieces of silver each to learn the secret of Samson's strength (Judges 16:5).
Samson lies to her three times (green withs, new ropes, weaving his hair into a loom) before finally revealing the Nazarite secret after she presses him 'unto death' (Judges 16:6-17).

verses.note: Introduced and bribed.
Extracts the true secret and has him captured.

characters.name: Micah

genealogy.note: Of Mount Ephraim (Judges 17:1). This section is framed by the refrain 'In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes' (Judges 17:6).

funFacts: Confesses to stealing 1,100 shekels of silver from his mother; she blesses him instead of cursing him and dedicates 200 shekels of it to a graven and molten image (Judges 17:2-4).

Consecrates one of his own sons as household priest, then replaces him with a hired wandering Levite, saying 'Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest' (Judges 17:5-13).

verses.note: The stolen silver and the idols.
Hires the young Levite as priest.
Loses his priest and idols to the Danites.

characters.name: Micah's Mother
characters.perkNote: Funds Micah's household idols and blesses rather than curses him.

genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout.

funFacts: Dedicates 200 of her 1,100 recovered shekels of silver to a graven and molten image for Micah's house (Judges 17:3-4).

verses.note: Her curse, blessing, and dedication of the silver.

characters.name: Jonathan the Levite
characters.perkNote: Ultimately leaves Micah's household for a better offer from the Danites, costing Micah both his priest and his idols.

children: unnamed sons, later priests of the Danite idol (Judges 18:30)
genealogy.note: Named only at Judges 18:30, as 'Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh.' The KJV's 'Manasseh' reflects a well-documented textual crux: the underlying Hebrew has a raised/suspended letter (nun) that many scholars believe was inserted to obscure an original reading of 'Moses,' avoiding a direct link between Moses' lineage and this idolatrous priesthood. The KJV's actual wording ('Manasseh') is used here as the primary datum; descent from Moses is flagged as a scholarly possibility, not asserted as fact. 'Gershom' itself also reuses a name found for Moses' own son (Exodus 2:22) and for Levi's son Gershon/Gershom (Genesis 46:11; 1 Chronicles 6:16-17). Also unrelated to the far more famous Jonathan, son of Saul.

funFacts: A young Levite 'of Bethlehemjudah, of the family of Judah' (Judges 17:7) — a Levite by tribe residing/sojourning within Judah's territory, not a claim that he belonged to the tribe of Judah.
Hired by Micah as household priest for 10 shekels of silver a year plus clothing and food (Judges 17:10).

Persuaded by 600 armed Danite men to become priest to the whole tribe of Dan instead — 'Is it better that thou shouldest be a priest unto the house of one man, or that thou be a priest unto a tribe and a family in Israel?' (Judges 18:19-20) — and takes Micah's ephod, teraphim, and graven image with him.
He and his sons served as priests of the Danite idol 'until the day of the captivity of the land' (Judges 18:30).

verses.note: Hired by Micah.
Persuaded to join the Danites.
Named and given his genealogy.

characters.name: The Levite of Mount Ephraim

genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout; identified only as 'a certain Levite sojourning on the side of mount Ephraim' (Judges 19:1).

funFacts: Takes a concubine from Bethlehemjudah; after she leaves him for her father's house, he goes to 'speak friendly unto her, and to bring her again' (Judges 19:1-3).
Refuses to lodge in Jebus (pre-conquest Jerusalem) because it was 'the city of a stranger,' choosing Gibeah of Benjamin instead — a fatal decision (Judges 19:11-15).
After the atrocity at Gibeah, divides his concubine's body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel's territory, precipitating the war against Benjamin (Judges 19:29-30).

verses.note: Introduced with his concubine.
Passes by Jebus and lodges in Gibeah.
Dismembers her body and summons Israel.

characters.name: The Levite's Concubine
characters.perkNote: Her death is the atrocity that drives the entire final tier of the book's narrative arc.

genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout.

funFacts: KJV Judges 19:2 states directly, 'And his concubine played the whore against him, and went away from him unto her father's house to Bethlehemjudah, and was there four whole months' — this is the KJV's own exact wording; some scholars and other versions render the underlying Hebrew differently (e.g., that she became angry or estranged rather than unfaithful), a genuine translation crux not resolved here.
Put out to the mob at Gibeah by the Levite; found dead or dying on the doorstep in the morning (Judges 19:25-27).

verses.note: Introduced; the KJV's description of her departure.
Her death at Gibeah.

characters.name: The Concubine's Father
characters.perkNote: His repeated hospitality delays the travelers' departure, shaping the timing of the whole tragedy.

genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout, 'her father' (Judges 19:4).

funFacts: Detains the Levite with lavish hospitality across several days: 'Tarry all night, and let thine heart be merry' (Judges 19:4-9).

verses.note: His repeated hospitality and delay of their departure.

characters.name: The Old Man of Gibeah
characters.perkNote: Takes the travelers in when no one else in Gibeah would, in a scene that closely echoes Lot's hospitality in Sodom (Genesis 19).

genealogy.note: Unnamed throughout; from Mount Ephraim but sojourning in Gibeah (Judges 19:16).

funFacts: The only person in Gibeah willing to take the travelers in for the night (Judges 19:16-21).

Offers his own virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine to the mob in place of his guest (Judges 19:23-24) — a deeply troubling episode the text presents without commentary, catalogued here factually rather than softened.

verses.note: Offers hospitality.
Confronts the mob.

characters.name: Phinehas

genealogy.note: Genealogy given (son of Eleazar, son of Aaron) matches the Phinehas of Numbers 25:7 and Joshua 22:13,30-32, suggesting continuity with the same individual; his appearance this late in Judges' closing appendix (chapters 17-21) is commonly read by scholars as chronologically earlier than the book's final placement would suggest, keeping him plausibly still alive — noted as a common observation, not asserted as settled internal chronology.

funFacts: Stands before the ark at Bethel when Israel inquires of the LORD before the third, decisive battle against Benjamin (Judges 20:27-28).

The war leaves only 600 Benjamite men alive, fled to the rock Rimmon (Judges 20:47); the other tribes, having vowed not to give their own daughters to Benjamin, provide wives by sparing 400 virgins of Jabeshgilead (Judges 21:8-14) and by having the Benjamites seize dancing daughters of Shiloh during a feast (Judges 21:19-23).

verses.note: Inquires of the LORD before the third battle.
The book's closing refrain: 'In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.'
